subject: barnstormerBiplane
pitch:
Category: Vehicle.
Subject: barnstormer biplane.
Style: whimsical.
reasoning:
I'm planning out the biplane structure as a full TypeScript module built with the SDK, setting up a root body joint along with joints for the propeller, rudder, elevators, and ailerons, even though this isn't a creature and most parts can stay as plain geometry objects.

I'm designing a whimsical, chubby barnstormer-style biplane with a wingspan around 9m, bright red and cream striped wings, a round smiley-faced engine cowling, and a pilot with a trailing scarf and goggles in an open cockpit. I'm also sketching a small grass-field base with a windsock, hay bale, and fuel barrels, aiming for roughly 200 parts and 500-700 lines of efficient code, and working out ground-level coordinates so the big whimsical wheels sit properly at y=0.

Now I'm planning the joint hierarchy — a root body joint, spinning propeller, rudder, elevators, and aileron joints across both wings — before building the fuselage shape through a series of lofted stations.

Setting loft station coordinates...

Finishing the lathe outline so it starts and ends on the axis, forming a closed solid loop, then placing it at the cowling position pointing forward. For decoration I'm thinking about where to add cartoon eyes, probably on the sides of the cowling rather than the front since the propeller occupies that space.

Placing the eyes using hit-tested decals at symmetric azimuths with a guard for null hits, then adding a smile decal lower on the front dome, reasoning through how the cowling's curvature and radius affect where each decal actually lands.

Good, that works for the propeller spinner face. I'll adjust the center point slightly to [0,1.5,1.2] for more consistent ray exits, though it's not critical. For the wings, I'm thinking of building each half as an extrusion of a planar airfoil outline, with span along x and chord running forward along z, giving thickness in the vertical direction.

Instead I'll build an explicit outline with manually placed points to get nicely rounded tips rather than relying on the generic corner-smoothing. I'm writing a helper function that generates the wing outline with arc-shaped tip corners, then setting thickness and bevel values, and designing the paint function to render cream fabric with red tip bands and darker rib-stitch lines spaced along the chord.

I'm also adding a circular roundel emblem on the wing surfaces using a separate textured plane part positioned just above the wing, oriented flat with the right axis and slight lift to avoid z-fighting.

Now I'm positioning the wings relative to the fuselage: upper wing attached near the body root at y=3.0 with slight forward stagger, lower wing lower at y=1.15 so it's mid-low on the fuselage, with cabane struts connecting the fuselage top to the upper wing for support, and figuring out where the pilot sits in the cockpit area.

For a whimsical touch, I'm considering adding a second front cockpit with a stuffed teddy bear passenger wearing goggles, and adjusting the upper wing position forward slightly so it still clears the cockpit visually while keeping the pilot's head visible behind the trailing edge.

Now I'm positioning the cabane struts connecting the fuselage top to the wing, offsetting them sideways from the centerline so they flank the cockpit rather than colliding with the bear figure.

For the interplane struts I'm placing them at x=±2.7, single bay like a Stearman, with front and rear positions set by the wing chords, plus diagonal cross wires between the strut tops and bottoms and flying wires down to the cabane for extra bracing.

Now I'm thinking through a fun whimsical color palette—cherry red fuselage, cream wings with red and yellow tips, and a brass cowling using the clockwork kit's metal material.

Actually I'll skip cel paints since metal and glow effects would clash with it, and instead use the plain SDK paint kit with grain, mottle, and countershade, plus the glow kit for a lantern on the barn post and maybe the cockpit light. For the fuselage I'm deciding against loft sectors since they're meant for sweep options, and instead writing a custom paint function that masks a cream stripe band based on normal direction and vertical position.

Now I'm adding a darker red belly shade where the normal points downward, a thin dark red edge along the cream stripe, and considering whimsical stitched patch decals plus maybe a painted name like "FLY" across the fuselage side.

I'm working out the text decal placement for "FLYING FIDDLESTICK" plus a tail number, figuring out the orientation so it reads correctly when viewed from the left flank by computing the viewer's right-hand direction relative to the up axis.

For the left side, the nose (+Z) appears toward the viewer's left, so reading left-to-right moves naturally toward the tail, which matches typical plane lettering. On the right side, I work out the mirrored case: viewer's right points toward +Z, so text reads toward the nose instead, which still reads fine as a real plane livery would.

Now I'm planning the decal details: a script-style "Dizzy Daisy" name using a bold italic serif/cursive font, plus a "No. 7" marking on the tail rudder, and setting up the vertical fin extrusion geometry with its side-view outline and thickness direction.

Still working out fin geometry...

Still defining rudder geometry...

Now I'm setting up the rudder as a joint on the body, then planning the horizontal stabilizer and elevators as separate pieces mounted on their own joints, with the stabilizer fixed and elevators hinged behind it near the tail.

I'm working out the mirrored thickness direction for each elevator half, then moving on to the tail wheel assembly with a strut and leaf spring, plus a skid capsule. Next I'm planning the main landing gear with V-struts connecting the fuselage to the axles, and tires built from torus geometry for the wheels.

For the wheel hubs, I'm deciding between a lathe shape or a simple cream cylinder with a spoke-pattern texture applied via circle geometry on the outer face, settling on dimensions around R=0.4 with tube radius 0.15 for a reasonable outer wheel size, and positioning the axle height for ground contact.

Now I'm working out the landing gear geometry: struts running from the fuselage underside down to the axle in a V-shape, with wheels positioned at x=±1.25 and set up as spinnable joints parented to the body.

Next I'm designing the propeller — a joint placed forward on the fuselage pointing along z, with two tapered blades extruded in the XY plane using a rounded outline that widens toward the tip before curving back in.

I'm adding a slight rotation to the blades for charm, using an angle-based helper function to compute each blade's orientation. For the spinner, I'm lathing a cone-and-hub shape in brass, and considering small exhaust stacks along the cowling's top sides—maybe even a few trailing cream-colored smoke puffs for whimsy, though I'm wary of them looking out of place.

I'm deciding to skip the floating smoke puffs and instead give the exhaust a curved cartoon pipe shape. For the pilot, I'm building a capsule-shaped body with a sphere head, leather cap and goggles, and a long striped scarf streaming behind using a wavy sweep path.

I realize the wavy scarf path would clip through the tail fin, so I'm shifting the trail sideways—offsetting x from 0.2 to 0.5 so it streams beside the fin rather than through it, adjusting the catmull points accordingly.

Now I'm designing the pilot: a chubby torso and head in the cockpit, a leather helmet, brass goggle cylinders with glowing lenses positioned on the forehead, and a whimsical touch like a big handlebar moustache for character.

Adding helmet and arm shapes...

Fuselage top lands around y=2.0, so I'm adding a cockpit coaming ring there with a dark recessed disc for the interior, giving the illusion of an open cockpit the pilot sits into, without using transparency.

For the windscreens, I'll keep colors flat and position small tilted brass-framed glass panels in front of each occupant — one near z=-0.72 for the pilot, avoiding collision with the bear's back, and another around z=0.5 for the bear — using a thin extruded trapezoid shape colored light blue for the glass.

Now I'm adding cowling details: a ring of brass rivets circling the engine cowling using a radial pattern of small spheres at z around 1.25 with radius 0.66, and considering a swept brass band to accent the cowling's edge.

Adding a gravity fuel tank cylinder across the wing with a brass cap. I'm also considering whimsical bunting or streamer banners strung between wing struts, but thinking it's simpler to skip the draped-wire approach and keep decorations minimal.

Building frames along the sagging path so flags hang downward with lean 180, facing along the flow direction, using a mix of colored flag textures picked randomly, and mirroring the setup for the right side with body-anchored joints.

Now I'm working out how many bunting cards total (two strings of 8 flags each, 16 cards), then placing wheel chocks, windsock, and barrels on a grass disc base. I'm figuring out the vertical alignment so the plane's wheels sit flush at y=0 while the base extends downward to the floor, keeping the lowest points touching ground as required.

I'm shaping the base as a lathed disc with a rounded edge, grassy on top and dirt-colored along the side, using a paint function that switches material based on surface normal. I'll also add a dirt runway strip extruded as a long rounded rectangle under the plane for visual grounding.

For extra detail, I'll scatter small grass-texture cards across the top surface, filtering by upward-facing normals and keeping minimum spacing so they don't overlap, though I need to think about whether they'd poke through the plane's wheels.

I need to exclude the runway footprint from the scatter zone, filtering out hits whose x and z fall within the strip's bounds, then add flower cards using a separate daisy texture for variety. For props, I'm positioning a windsock pole while checking it stays clear of the plane's wingspan and within the base's radius.

Now I'm working out the windsock itself: a tapered cone shape with a horizontal axis, painted with alternating red and white stripe bands based on height, built using a lathe or sweep profile that droops slightly for a wavy flag effect.

Then I'm placing scene dressing: a mounting ring and striped pole with a ball top, two bulgy barrels with stripe paint off to the side, and a stack of hay bales made from a textured box, all checked against the circular base radius and wing clearance so nothing overlaps.

I'm also adding a hand-painted wooden sign with "AIR SHOW TODAY! 5¢ RIDES" text on a textured plane, angled toward the viewer and mounted on posts, plus a warm glowing lantern hanging from the sign post and small red/green navigation light spheres at the wingtips for extra storytelling detail.

Now I'm planning the plane's decorative textures: a cartoon eye and smile on the cowling, "Dizzy Daisy" lettering on each side of the fuselage, a sunburst star roundel on the wing, vertical pinstripe ribs along the wing panels, and a big star numeral on the tail, aiming for around six to nine distinct textures total.

I'm also considering a small cockpit instrument panel with a gauge texture imported from the clockwork kit, positioned just ahead of the windscreen and facing the pilot, since the plane faces forward along +Z.

Now I'm starting to lay out the actual builder calls, beginning with the biplane root body joint and working through the API details needed to verify each joint placement and orientation as I go.

I'm working through the fuselage loft, passing the body bone and station array, and considering whether default section shape and width/height interpolation fit without extra params. I'm also thinking through how the loft path's orientation frame determines which axis the width runs along, deciding to route the path from tail to nose.

For the fuselage paint function, I'm defining a shader that picks belly, side, or stripe colors based on normal direction and vertical position, but realizing the stripe band needs to shift since the fuselage centerline tapers toward the tail rather than staying level.

Still writing paint logic...

Writing wing outline geometry...

For wingtips I'll round them chunky with r≈0.55 for a plump, whimsical look while keeping taper simple rather than aerodynamic. I'm setting extrusion directions for the wing outline, centering it at the given origin, and picking thickness/bevel values (around 0.13 thickness, 0.045-0.06 bevel) so the cross-section looks rounded without needing a real airfoil shape, then double-checking the normal axes line up correctly.

Now I'm writing the paint function that colors the wing based on lateral position — red near the tip, cream in the middle, a narrow yellow band, plus thin ribs and a leading-edge stripe for detail, using face normals to restrict ribs to top/bottom surfaces only.

Adding more wing panel details...

I'm deciding to skip actual aileron geometry and just paint them on. For the roundel emblem, I'm placing it on the upper wing near the leading edge, oriented flush against the curved surface with a slight lift to avoid z-fighting, and skipping the underside decal for simplicity.

Now I'm adding a cylindrical fuel tank lying along the x-axis on top of the fuselage, with a brass cap and a red/cream painted band. I'm also planning the cabane and interplane struts, going with turquoise to match the cowling and thin dark wires, positioning the interplane struts at the wing roots.

Working out strut geometry...

Adding wire struts next...

Now I'm designing the landing gear: V-shaped legs attaching from the fuselage down to an axle, inclined outward for a realistic stance, with a brass-colored capsule fairing wrapped around the axle rod.

I'm also adding small bungee-cord style shock coils wound around the upper portion of each front leg, using a spiral sweep path with a thin radius and dark color for contrast. Next I'll move on to the wheels.

For each side, I'm setting up a wheel joint with a torus tyre and cylindrical hub, visible only on the outward face. I'm sizing the tyre torus so its outer radius sits the axle just above ground level with a dark rubber tone, then fitting a slightly narrower cylindrical hub recessed into the tyre's width so the tread sticks out on both sides.

Skipping wheel pants. Now working on the tail wheel assembly: a small torus wheel with a leaf-spring strut running from the fuselage tail down to the wheel, sketching the curve path points and sweep radius for the brass strut geometry.

For the tail wheel I'm orienting the torus axis along x and checking that it just touches the floor with a slight sink for realism, matching the main gear's sink depth. Then I'm moving on to the cowling, building it as a lathe shape around the fuselage's z-axis with an outline profile defining its rounded nose contour.

Refining the cowling profile points...

Now I'm figuring out the z-positions: cowling front around z=1.89, prop joint at 1.9, spinner extending to 2.2, blades at 1.95. I'm checking that the cowling bulges wider than the fuselage nose for a whimsical look, and adjusting the fuselage station dimensions to smooth the transition into that larger cowling ring.

Now I'm placing a rounded cowling flange, then working out the eye decals -- sizing them around 0.3-0.36 to fit the dome's 0.69 radius, positioning them at roughly ±32° azimuth and 28° elevation, and thinking through how the decal projection's direction and up-vector will orient the eyes correctly on the curved surface.

I want the eyes to read undistorted as if viewed from the front, so I'm setting an explicit projection direction tilted slightly rather than relying purely on the surface normal at the hit point, and passing both the hit location and a custom direction/size for the decal. Next I'm moving on to placing the mouth as a smile near a similar azimuth position.

For the mouth texture I'm considering combining it with blush cheek ellipses into a single wider decal region rather than separate decals, keeping the canvas compact. I also need to check that the spinning propeller blades at rest angle don't visually block the face features given their width and rotation offset.

Thinking through blade placement, I want the blades angled horizontally-ish, tilted around 10 degrees from horizontal, so they pass between the eyes (around y +0.3) and mouth (around y -0.3) rather than occluding either feature directly.

Now I'm adding exhaust stacks to the cowling sides, sweeping tapered pipes from near the cowl back along the fuselage, using a dark brass metal finish for the collector pipes.

Switching focus to the pilot figure now—placing it in the rear cockpit, working out the fuselage top height at that station and positioning a cockpit disc just above the loft surface to seat the figure properly.

I'll instead build a dished cockpit rim as a solid lathe-shaped tub sitting slightly proud of the fuselage, spanning from y 1.8 to 2.06, so the dark top disc and brown rim blend smoothly into the hull without visible gaps.

Now I'm positioning the pilot figure: a torso capsule sitting in the cockpit tub with its base tucked inside the fuselage, topped by a head sphere, keeping proportions so the whole pilot peaks around y=2.8 once the helmet is added.

For the pilot's face, I'm adding a nose, goggle lenses positioned symmetrically on the head surface using the sphere geometry to find the right z-offset, plus a strap band circling the head to hold the goggles in place.

Now I'm shaping a handlebar moustache using a curved path that sweeps outward and curls upward on each side, colored a ginger brown tone with rounded caps for a classic pilot look.

For the helmet, I'm adding a partial-sphere leather cap with flattened ear flaps on each side and a forehead goggle strap, using a sphere clipped to a hemisphere shape for the cap.

Then for the teddy bear character, I'm planning its own torso capsule, larger head sphere, ears, snout, nose, and eyes, possibly giving it a bow tie and pushed-up goggles for a matching cheerful aviator look.

I'm now checking the bear's head position relative to the windscreen and upper wing clearances, and making sure the cabane struts near the cockpit tub don't collide with the bear's seating position or the pilot's windscreen behind it.

Now I'm laying out the instrument panel between the pilot's tub and windscreen, positioning a small leather-covered box with a gauge circle mounted on its rear face.

For the windscreens I'm planning a trapezoid glass pane extruded with light blue-tinted material, plus a brass rod across the top to serve as a frame rather than a full frame structure, keeping things simple with a flat vertical orientation and base around y=2.0. Next I want to add a name decal along the fuselage side.

Finding placement is tricky since most of the mid-body is occupied by the cockpit tub and wing roots, so I'm thinking the rear fuselage near z=-2.2 gives enough flat area—sizing the text around 1.3 by 0.28 spanning roughly z=-2.9 to -1.6 at y=1.62, which should fit within the fuselage's narrower rear section without clashing with the tub above.

For the tail number on the rudder, I'm thinking of positioning a flat textured plane offset slightly from the rudder's extruded face rather than decaling directly onto it, oriented so its normal faces outward along the side direction and its up axis aligns for readable text orientation.

Checking the cross product math confirms the text direction runs correctly toward the tail for each side, with the viewer's right matching the expected reading direction on both the positive and negative side cases. Now I'm thinking through the rudder's physical thickness to position the plane with proper offset.

For the whimsical touches I'm planning a circled "7" decal for the rudder, plus considering a flower decal for the tail fin. I'm now writing SVG markup for an eye texture with a white ellipse, dark pupil, highlights, and eyelash detail.

Writing mouth and smile texture...

For the name texture, I'm planning an italic serif "Dizzy Daisy" title with a cream fill and dark outline stroke using paint-order, plus small star swashes, rendered large at 512px for crispness.

Now I'm designing the roundel texture with concentric red, cream, and turquoise rings plus a yellow five-point star, then the wheel hub with a cream circle, six red spokes, a brass ring, and a center cap. For the flag texture I'm working out how a pennant hangs from the frame with a 180-degree lean so it reads upside down, with its root edge attached at the bottom.

Writing pennant SVG path...

Then I'm sketching grass and flower textures with root points anchored at the bottom, varying card sizes between 0.18 and 0.3, and starting on the sign texture viewBox.

Now I'm designing the sign with a wooden plank background and carnival text like "AIR SHOW" and "RIDES 5¢" in dark red, plus a gauge texture for the altimeter dial. Counting up all the textures — eye, smile, name, roundel, hub, flags, grass, two flower variants, sign, gauge — I'm at 14, which feels like too many, so I'm considering trimming the flag variants down to three to stay closer to the target range.

Rather than separate textures for grass and two flower types, I'm merging them into fewer images: one plain grass tuft texture and one combined tuft-with-daisy texture, since each card shows the whole drawing anyway. I'm also thinking through how tinting works — since colored tints apply over greyscale drawings, I want the daisy petals greyscale so they tint properly, but the stem would need to stay a believable green rather than getting tinted an odd color, so I'm settling on a single daisy texture drawn mostly in color with just the petals left tintable.

For the flag, instead of tinting a grey pennant per card (which would multiply into separate atlas entries anyway), I'm using one multi-colored striped pennant texture so it only costs a single slot. That brings the texture count to ten total: eye, smile, name, roundel, hub, flag, grass, daisy, sign, and gauge.

Now I'm listing out all the paint/material categories needed — fuselage, wing, cowling, tail surfaces, grass, runway, wood grain, tyres, barrel, hay, pole stripes, windsock stripes, prop — and estimating the total part count lands around 200, which seems reasonable. Time to start writing the code.

I'm setting up imports carefully, pulling in only the builder functions and kit helpers I'll actually use since unused imports could fail typechecking, and I'm defining a type-safe helper function for generating rounded rectangle outlines as coordinate arrays.

I'm hoping the SDK drops exact-duplicate consecutive points automatically, relying on trig producing exact floating-point equality at these corner boundaries.

For safety I'll cap radius to chord/2 minus a small margin to avoid degenerate zero-length edges triggering self-intersection checks. Then I move to the wing plan, defining the extrude outline with lateral x and chordwise y, using the rounded-rectangle helper with the leading edge positioned along +y.

Now I'm setting up the color palette constants (reds, teals, creams, leather tones) and starting the build function that assembles the model's parts.

I'm defining the body joint, propeller joint with hinge-free orientation, and giving hinge roles to rudder and elevators instead. Then I'm starting on the fuselage stations array, laying out positions and widths along the body's length.

Checking that the loft path moves monotonically in z and considering tail cone shaping, then sketching a cockpit helper function using a lathe profile for the canopy rim shape.

Checking the disc placement sits just above the dish floor, confirming it fits within bounds. Now I'm working out the pilot/torso construction, settling on using rod or capsule helpers with explicit color and bone options to build the limb segments safely according to the API signatures.

For the head, I'm adding a stylized sphere with skin color at the appropriate height, debating whether to use flat shading for a faceted look versus smooth shading, and leaning toward keeping the head smooth for a cuter effect while reserving flat shading for other parts. I'm now working out the arm geometry, positioning shoulders and hands so the pilot appears to reach forward toward the control stick.

Positioning the control stick with a tilted rod and a red knob sphere, then placing glove-colored hand spheres near the grip point. I check that the stretched-forward arms don't awkwardly intersect the head, and move on to planning a scarf ring around the neck.

Adding the scarf torus around the neck with red striping, then sketching a ribbon sweep for the trailing end using a tapering width curve, alternating red and cream color stripes along its length via a catmull path.

I'm reconsidering ribbon orientation since the default tube frame would make it either flat horizontal or standing vertical depending on which axis gets the wide radius — going with the horizontal flat look as more natural for a flowing scarf tail, with the wave varying in y and offset slightly in x to avoid clipping the fin.

I'm now plotting the ribbon's path points so it stays clear of the fin geometry near x=0.2-0.5 across the z range where the fin sits, checking that its spread stays wide enough to pass clean above or alongside other features like the wing.

Next I'm sketching the bear's anatomy: placing a torso rod, head sphere, snout with a scaled sphere and dark nose, rounded ears with pink inner detail, and small black eye spheres, all positioned relative to the z-coordinate along the body.

I'm deciding to skip the goggles-on-forehead idea and instead give the bear a simple red bow tie at the neck, then define the raised waving arm with a rod and paw sphere, and starting the resting arm on the rim.

Now I'm assembling the wings as extruded rounded shapes positioned above and below the body, bevel-checking the thickness, and defining a wingPaint function that colors the wing surface based on span and chord with upper/lower variation.

Refining the paint logic: coloring the tip region red with a thin yellow stripe marking the transition, then shading the leading edge red along the forward outline, and carving out an aileron region near the trailing edge further defined by position along the span.

Placing tip glow spheres on the upper wingtips with red for +X and green for −X, then working out interplane strut positions connecting the lower wing's top surface to the upper wing's underside at front and rear chord points.

Now figuring out the cross-bracing wires between strut endpoints, and considering flying wires from the cabane struts out to the strut bottoms—trying to avoid routing them through the wing itself.

Checking the cabane strut positions against fuselage cross-sections at both the front and rear attachment heights to make sure they land right at the edge of the hull.

Now I notice the rear strut base is floating .17 outside the actual surface, so I'm adjusting its placement inward, but that creates a conflict with the tub/bear fairing radius around the rear fuselage — moving the strut forward to avoid overlap just shifts the collision elsewhere. I'll try repositioning the upper wing's z-center instead to resolve the clash geometrically.

Checking the resulting chord range and verifying the rear cabane clears both the bear tub and pilot tub fronts now with some margin. I'm also working out placement for the windscreen and instrument panel in the gap between the pilot tub and the bear tub, then figuring out the fuselage half-width at the cabane's rear attachment point to size the strut base correctly.

I'm finalizing the cabane strut endpoints front and rear, then locking in the wing chord ranges and centers for both upper and lower wings, plus the front and rear strut z-positions to keep everything within the fuselage bounds.

Now I'm nudging the rear upper wing edge inward slightly, placing the fuel tank behind the upper wing center, and working out roundel placement on the top wing surface—skipping the lower wing roundel since it's underside-flipped. I'm also starting on the tail stabilizer's rounded plan outline and position.

Still shaping the elevator outlines...

I'm defining the elevator polygon manually so the two halves overlap slightly at the center pivot, then checking the stabilizer outline spans correctly so the elevator's pivot and tip width roughly match the stab's depth.

For paint, I'm setting the elevator and stab to red with cream ribs, using a periodic function along the lateral coordinate to generate stripe lines. Then I'm starting on the fin, extruding it at a forward position with a swept outline that leans back toward the tail.

Now I'm shaping the rudder itself, extending from the fin's trailing edge with its own tapered outline, checking that its top height stays near the fin's peak and its lower portion clears the fuselage end. I'm placing the rudder's hinge joint and planning a "7" decal on its sides, then moving to paint the fin red with a cream stripe near the top.

For the rudder paint, I'm dividing the outline into horizontal bands - red, cream, teal - for a patriotic stripe pattern, and deciding to skip a custom number decal in favor of reusing the roundel texture on the cream band to avoid extra texture atlas work. Now I'm moving on to the cowling after finishing the landing gear logic.

Next I'm working out the exhaust stacks: shaping a tapered brass metal path with a swept radius that curves outward from the cowling, checking that the geometry clears the fuselage sides at each height so the stacks sit properly beside the body without clipping through it.

Now I'm setting up a ring of rivets around the fuselage using evenly spaced frames facing outward along the circumference, then figuring out which bone each rivet should attach to—since the ring frames don't inherently carry bone data, I need to determine the nearest joint, likely resolving to the body-to-propeller bone that spans that section of the fuselage.

Now I'm defining the base's lathe outline with ground-level thickness and bone assignment, adding a grass/dirt paint split by normal, then extruding a thin runway strip on top positioned to align with the lathe's surface height.

For the runway surface, I'm shaping a rounded rectangular outline sized to fit within the base's circular footprint, painting a mottled tan with darker tire-track stripes using the top face's coordinate system, and planning wedge-shaped chocks near the wheel positions using an extruded triangular profile.

Now adding two wooden barrels nearby, checking their distances fit the layout, and setting up a lathe-style outline with painted dark bands near the top and bottom for a weathered look.

Next I'm building hay bale shapes with a yellow-brown grain texture and thin darker straps wrapped around them, then placing two stacked bales and double-checking their positions keep roughly consistent spacing from neighboring objects.

For the windsock pole, I'm working out a striped red-and-white rod rising to 3.3m with stripes calculated along its length, then mounting the sock at the top and bending it outward with a bezier curve to indicate wind direction.

Now I'm working out the sign design: two support posts flanking a wooden board positioned around (3.9, 1.35, 3.5), with the board oriented to face the path direction and a texture plane mounted in front for the lettering.

I'm also adding a hanging lantern on top of the right post—a small cage cylinder with a glowing yellow sphere inside—to light the sign at night.

Now I'm scattering grass tufts and daisies across the base surface, filtering hits to avoid overlapping with the sign posts and other props by defining exclusion zones around each prop's position and radius.

For the card placement, I'm sizing the grass blades with slight lean and spin variation, attaching them rigidly to the body bone, and giving them an upward flow direction for natural orientation. Then I'm working out the flag bunting positions, running a sagging path from the wing struts near the cabane to create a catenary-like curve for the hanging flags.

Now I'm trying different placements for the bunting wire relative to the leading edge of the upper wing, but the geometry keeps looking awkward hanging below it. I'm considering simpler alternatives—maybe running the festoon along the lower wing's leading edge or attaching it to the landing gear instead.

Defining bunting curve and flags...

I need to work out decal targeting for textured cards and the cowling lathe part, using surface hit-testing to find the correct placement point for details like eyes—falling back to non-null assertions when a hit should always exist. For mirrored features like eye pupils, I'll apply a mirror flag based on side to keep the texture roughly symmetrical.

Still refining eye artwork...

Now I'm working out the leg and coil geometry for the figure, computing positions for the front legs relative to the fuselage center and half-height to make sure the bottom aligns properly.

Working out wheel placement so the hub, tire, and axle don't overlap — setting wheels at x=±1.35 with axle ends matching, strut bottoms at ±1.1, and checking tire torus and hub cap offsets so the outer faces clear each other by a small margin.

Naming the wheel joints by side (L/R based on sign of x) and setting their parent body, position, and rotation axis to match the wheel orientation. Then moving on to the propeller spinner and starting the windscreen function — defining a glass pane extruded from an outline, positioned above the body with a thin thickness for the vertical windshield.

Adding the brass frame rods around the windscreen edges (top and sides), then adjusting the base width and height so it fits the fuselage curvature near the pilot's position, accounting for the surface being lower at the sides than at the center.

Next I'm placing the instrument panel box just behind the windscreen, positioning the gauge circles embedded in it with proper depth and spacing, reusing a single gauge texture for both dials, and checking that everything clears the pilot tub and the bear's reaching hands. I'm also starting to place the bear's eyes as small black spheres.

Now I'm setting up a reusable `part` helper that wraps `b.part` with a default bone body, allowing overrides via spread, before moving into writing the propeller blade geometry with symmetric left/right offsets and rotation angles.

Writing blade geometry...

I'm shaping the blade outline to be a bit chubby and whimsical, coloring the tip brass past a threshold and using a wood grain paint elsewhere, then double-checking the joint direction property, texture option on part, and that rng properly returns a seeded function for scatter calls.
